name: Zoe Weber

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government, and we don't sell or campaign. What you tell me is confidential, including anything different from a public answer. Could you describe your normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Zoe, 43, and I lead an electrical crew wiring homes and repairing business premises. I've got a two-year technical diploma and a master electrician's licence, and I'm among the people the firm trusts most with a difficult fault. Today I found why an old shop circuit kept failing, then stayed with a younger worker until the testing made sense. I like a pencil mark on a drawing and dislike being asked to approve a job I haven't had time to check.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What should I know about the household and your way of handling change?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner works as a school caretaker, and our children are ten and fourteen. We've got a mortgage, eight months of normal expenses saved, higher pay than usual from my job and plenty of electrical firms nearby. I never use AI tools and take time to understand any replacement for a familiar method. I don't feel I have to take a side in the argument; I want the real task, wage and cost in front of me.

say: I'd welcome a **quieter working year** while letting the office make invoices easier.
I'd keep explaining **actual tests** instead of asking a younger worker to copy a number.
think: The **good wage and reserve** make ordinary household bills feel secure in this mild picture.
I can do **worthwhile familiar work** without needing to change careers to prove I noticed the future.
do: Continue leading **electrical jobs** with the paper test book through the first plateau year.
Keep the **household budget** and final checks rather than spend existing reserves on an unnecessary new system.
feel: **Calm** about household living, with ordinary work frustrations separate from fear of losing income.
S0.quote: A customer gets a safe repair from the work, not from my confidence in a sentence.
fieldNote: Her **calm** reflects high pay, a substantial reserve and many local alternatives, while high technical skill appears in difficult faults and teaching.
She retains **familiar methods** and existing savings, without treating routine work or held cash as a newly chosen training or saving action.

steps.text: Continue leading ordinary electrical jobs with paper records and final checks

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew I could enjoy a quieter year of doing the work. The office could make invoices easier without asking me to replace the book I understood. I'd still explain the test to the younger worker rather than hand over a number to copy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our work and money would feel secure in that picture. The good wage covers the ordinary bills, and eight months put aside gives us room for an interruption. I wouldn't need a change of career to feel I was doing something worthwhile.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd keep leading the usual electrical jobs and using my paper test book. Through the first plateau year I'd keep the ordinary household budget and ask for the same final checks before handover. I wouldn't spend the reserve on a new system just because the news had become quieter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, with relief that I could get better at familiar work instead of chasing every announcement. I'd still get tired and cross with a late delivery. That wouldn't mean I was frightened for our household living.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if a customer wanted an immediate answer before the checks?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask what the customer needed explained and show the actual test record. I wouldn't pretend a quick answer was the same as a checked installation. A customer gets a safe repair from the work, not from my confidence in a sentence.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use more of the reserve in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd leave it available rather than treat it as money that had suddenly become spare. It's the reserve we already built, not new saving caused by a quieter forecast. It would still matter if ordinary business went through a bad spell.

say: I'd ask what **paid work changes** before the firm changes the crew rota.
I'd seek one **practical shared request** about instructions and pay without demanding agreement about every tool.
think: I expect both **physical wages** to hold over the next few years.
New coordination expectations could still consume **unpaid evenings**, even while the household wage remains secure.
do: Invite willing leads to a **shared written request** for duties, paid coordination and weekly pay now.
Keep **paper work records** during the first year, using internal task details to show required calls outside paid hours.
feel: **Uneasy** about hours and instructions, while secure about household bills and willing to request clear terms.
S1.quote: A friendly conversation wouldn't be an agreement.
fieldNote: She distinguishes **secure income** from concern about unpaid coordination, rather than treating every disliked office change as expected job loss.
The **joint request** uses willing colleagues and internal task records, while written terms are required before she relies on any changed arrangement.

steps.text: Seek written duties, paid coordination and weekly pay with willing leads, relying only on written agreement
Keep paper repair records and internal notes of required calls outside paid hours

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the firm should tell us what paid work was actually changing before changing the rota. I'd ask the other crew leads to join one practical request about instructions and pay. We wouldn't need to agree about every tool to agree that work takes paid time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect my physical repair wage and my partner's caretaker wage to hold over the next few years. But I'd be uneasy about a new plan moving coordination calls into the evening while claiming the day had got shorter. I don't want a secure wage used as a reason not to count the hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd ask the other leads to sign a shared request for written duties, paid coordination and weekly pay. During the first year I'd keep the paper repair records and note any required calls outside paid hours, using only internal task details. I'd take those examples to the owner with willing colleagues rather than speak for people who hadn't agreed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about the working day, but not afraid that the mortgage was about to beat us. I'd want a plain answer about who did the coordination. I wouldn't need to be enthusiastic about software to make that request.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the firm required an unfamiliar electronic record?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask for paid instruction and a checked first record before being required to send it. I wouldn't guess to make the transition look smooth. Knowing the electrical job and knowing a new screen are different pieces of work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make the paid-time request a real agreement?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask for the written terms and read the weekly pay and hours before relying on them. A friendly conversation wouldn't be an agreement. I wouldn't put a proposed shorter day into the family calendar.

say: I'd separate **2028 thinking work** from robots around 2031 and ask what paid lead duties remain.
I wouldn't treat a **difficult old building** as a guarantee of the same wage for a whole career.
think: Both **physical household jobs** could lose hours as capable robots approach.
Our **eight-month reserve** gives time to examine options, without replacing wages for the rest of the mortgage.
do: Save **100 monthly** from new wages only if essentials leave that amount spare and neither wage has fallen.
Maintain **shared request** for written duties, paid coordination and weekly pay with willing leads, counting no agreement before written terms.
Keep **paid repairs** after 2028, reviewing actual wages monthly and stopping extra transfers if either saving condition fails.
feel: **Anxious** about possible income loss, with savings and nearby employers providing room to examine choices.
S2.quote: A tidy monthly savings transfer isn't worth making an essential bill difficult.
fieldNote: The **new cash saving** comes from future wages, stops after either wage falls or surplus disappears, and never relabels existing reserves.
Her **course questions** remain questions, while work and pay proposals remain unagreed until written terms rather than assumed protections.

steps.text: Save 100 monthly only from spare new wages after essentials, if neither wage has fallen
Seek written duties, paid coordination and weekly pay with willing leads, relying only on written agreement
Keep paid repairs after 2028; stop extra transfers if either wage falls or surplus disappears

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew thinking work changes in 2028 and capable hands-on robots follow around 2031. I'd keep doing the paid repairs while asking what duties the firm would actually need. A difficult old building isn't a promise about the rest of my working life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My hours could shrink as capable robots approached, and my partner's physical job could change too. Eight months of expenses would give us time to choose, not a replacement wage for a long mortgage. I'd be anxious about needing unfamiliar work before I'd had time to understand it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd add 100 monthly from new wages to cash savings only if essentials left that amount spare and neither wage had fallen. I'd continue the shared request for written duties, paid coordination and weekly pay with willing leads, relying on no agreement before written terms. In the first year after 2028 I'd keep paid repairs and check both actual wages monthly, stopping the extra transfer if those conditions failed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about possible lost income, but able to do something without emptying the reserve or rushing into a course. I'd have money and nearby firms to examine. I wouldn't confuse having time to look with already having found another wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if either wage fell or an essential cost increased?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop the extra transfer rather than borrow or draw from the eight months to keep the target alive. It would be new wage money or no transfer. A tidy monthly savings transfer isn't worth making an essential bill difficult.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you pay for retraining immediately?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I'd need the actual work, paid hours, costs and practical teaching before choosing a course. I'd ask those questions rather than enrol to calm myself down. I wouldn't call a question an earning plan.

say: I'd use **five years** to check actual duties before buying a preparation promise.
I'd keep **robots around 2034** visible without treating the warning itself as a paid opportunity.
think: I expect more years of **steady household income** while practical work remains needed.
At **48 in 2031**, I would still need earnings beyond the later arrival of capable robots.
do: Maintain **shared request** for written duties, paid coordination and weekly pay with willing leads, counting no agreement before written terms.
Save **100 monthly** from new wages only if essentials leave it spare and neither wage has fallen.
Keep **paid repairs** after 2031 and review wages monthly, stopping extra transfers if either condition fails.
feel: **Uneasy** about later earning needs, while secure about near-term household living and able to ask careful questions.
S3.quote: I can compare a job offer without applying or resigning.
fieldNote: The **slower timeline** changes near-term income expectations, without removing the same eventual machines or her ongoing need for wages.
She keeps **course and job comparisons** distinct from chosen actions, while new saving remains conditional on unchanged wages and a real surplus.

steps.text: Seek written duties, paid coordination and weekly pay with willing leads, relying only on written agreement
Save 100 monthly only from spare new wages after essentials, if neither wage has fallen
Keep paid repairs after 2031; stop extra transfers if either wage falls or surplus disappears

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years gives us time to check an actual new duty before buying something meant to prepare us for it. I'd still keep robots around 2034 in view. More time doesn't turn an untested promise into a paid job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Compared with 2028, I expect several more years of steady household income while the work is mainly practical. That gives me time to understand a real requirement without making the reserve our main wage. I'd still need earnings after 2031, when I'd be 48.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd keep the shared request for written duties, paid coordination and weekly pay and continue the 100 monthly cash transfer only from new wages, if essentials left it spare and neither wage had fallen. In the first year after 2031 I'd keep the repair job and review actual household wages monthly. I'd stop the extra transfer if either wage fell or essential costs used the spare amount.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about the later career, but secure about the household over the next few years. I'd want room to ask for a second demonstration if a method was new to me. I wouldn't suddenly become an AI user because the deadline had moved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you need before considering a course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd write down the task and ask the employer who would teach it, what time was paid and what the course actually cost. I haven't enrolled or chosen to fund anything just by asking. I'd want the terms before risking time or money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you begin a job search automatically?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd compare any actual offer with written pay, hours, duties and travel before making a choice. I can compare a job offer without applying or resigning. I'd keep the current wage until there was a decision worth making.

I'd keep seeking **written paid duties** without directing the children to copy my trade.
think: At **53 in 2036**, I couldn't assume retirement income, adult children's wages or a cleared mortgage.
Present pay, the **reserve and local options** make the next few years secure while later choices remain uncertain.
do: Maintain **shared request** for written duties, paid coordination and weekly pay with willing leads, counting no agreement before written terms.
Save **100 monthly** from new wages only if essentials leave it spare and neither wage has fallen.
Keep **paid repairs** after 2036, reviewing wages monthly and stopping extra transfers if either condition fails.
feel: **Uneasy** about eventual career changes, while secure about near-term living and able to enjoy current family time.
S4.quote: Careful waiting should still involve looking at the figures.
fieldNote: She **ages both children** before discussing their choices, counting neither adult wages nor an assumed pension as household resources.
Her **new-saving conditions** survive the long horizon, with immediate review after a changed wage rather than reliance on a distant date.

steps.text: Seek written duties, paid coordination and weekly pay with willing leads, relying only on written agreement

Keep paid repairs after 2036; stop extra transfers if either wage falls or surplus disappears

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade lets us make decisions when the real tasks and offers become visible. I'd keep asking for written paid duties, not a reassuring new title. I wouldn't ask the children to copy a familiar job just because their mother knew it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be 53 at the thinking change in 2036 and around 56 when robots followed. The children would be twenty and twenty-four in 2036, but I couldn't assume they were earning or that our mortgage had disappeared. Our present pay, reserve and many nearby employers still make the next few years secure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now I'd maintain the shared request for written duties, paid coordination and weekly pay and save 100 monthly only from new wages if essentials left it spare and neither wage had fallen. In the first year after 2036 I'd keep paid repairs and review actual wages and bills monthly with my partner. I'd stop the extra transfer if either wage fell or the spare amount disappeared, rather than draw from the existing reserve.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about the eventual career, but able to enjoy the family we have now. I'd have time to understand a real choice rather than buy a general answer. I wouldn't count being in my fifties as having a pension.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you assume about the children at those future ages?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I wouldn't put either adult child's possible wage into our budget or choose their studies from this card. I'd help read an actual paid-learning offer if they asked. Their future work would be their decision, not a way to settle my mortgage worry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would keep the long preparation from becoming delay?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd compare actual paid duties and household wages with the written terms each year. If either wage changed earlier, we'd review immediately rather than wait for 2036. Careful waiting should still involve looking at the figures.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because repair hours could shrink before I'd understood a real next duty. Written weekly pay, hours and responsibilities, with paid practical instruction for any actual new task, would help. Eight months of savings lets me ask a slower question without pretending I already know the answer.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask whether the person is waiting because there is no real offer to inspect yet. I don't like unnecessary risk, but I can read a wage and a task list. I'd rather make a careful decision than announce a change I haven't chosen.

headlineQuote: Eight months of savings lets me ask a slower question without pretending I already know the answer.
portrait: **Zoe, 43**, leads electrical crews with a two-year technical diploma and a master electrician's licence.
Her **high trade pay**, eight-month reserve and many local employers support a household with partner, two schoolchildren and mortgage.
She **never uses AI**, prefers familiar methods and seeks clear paid duties with willing colleagues rather than promises about new titles.
Her **cash transfers** require new wage surplus and unchanged wages; future courses, job changes and children's earnings are never assumed.
Fast change brings **anxiety** about hours; longer warnings leave current bills secure while she remains uneasy about later work.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could cut repair hours before she understands the next real paid responsibility.
whatWouldHelp: Written weekly **pay and hours**, alongside actual duties, would clarify the job.
**Paid practical instruction** for a real new task would let her learn without relying on reassurance.
